# dsh-qqbot-bridge
**English** · 简体中文
> Route QQ private messages into the AI team sessions you **already** have in DeepSeek Harness — sam
e session id, same memory, same permissions. No second QQ gateway, no copy-pasted system prompt.
*Real run: a private message on QQ, answered by the Bot's actual DSH session — code, files and all.
The same conversation is waiting in the DSH Web UI.*
[代码示例省略，未执行]
## The problem

You already run a **team of agents** inside DSH: several Bots, each with its own long-lived
session,

its own role instructions, its own long-term memory, its own tools and workspace.
You want to talk
to them **from QQ**.

The obvious approach — *"write a QQ bot that calls the model with the same system prompt"* —
silentl

y throws away everything that made the team worth building: the conversation history,
the memory fil

es, the permissions, the workspace, the resume-after-restart behaviour.
You end up with a stranger w
earing the same name.

This project does not do that. It **delivers a QQ message into the session that Bot already
has**, a
nd relays the Bot's answer back to QQ.
## What makes it different
| | Typical QQ ⇄ LLM bridge | **dsh-qqbot-bridge** |
| Identity | Copies the system prompt | **Reuses the real session** — `sessionController.resolveAgen

t(sessionId)` then `agent.followup(createUserMessage({ source }))` |
| Context | Starts from scratch

| The Bot's actual history, memory, tools and workspace |
| Web ⇄ QQ | Two disconnected worlds | **

One session**: start on QQ, continue in the Web UI, same context |
| QQ gateway | Opens its own conn
ection | **Borrows** the one the official plugin already runs — no second login, no credential race

|
| Allowlist | `[]` often means *everyone* | `[]` means **nobody** (fail-closed); refused peers are

only *recorded*, never auto-granted |
| Observability | Silence when it breaks | Console lines **an

d** `bridge-status.json` — "did it load?" always has an answer |
| Official commands | Frequently sw

allowed | `/bot-ping`, `/bot-status`, … keep working |
| Long conversations | Pins one session id |
Re-reads `state.json` before every send, so a session that rolls over to a new part keeps working |
| Group chats | Often on by default | Off, and group traffic is handed back to the stock chain untou
p chats | Often on by default | Off, and group traffic is handed back to the stock chain untouched |
Every row above is backed by a test or a real run log — see `TEST-REPORT.md`.
## How it works
[代码示例省略，未执行]

The bridge registers **one** Cordis service of its own (`qqbotBridge`) so an operator can ask
a live
host what it is doing.
### Why a fork of the QQ plugin is required

The stock `@tencent-connect/dsh-qqbot` keeps its `QQBot` instance, `SessionManager` and
outbound sen

der inside local variables and **registers no Cordis service at all**, so an
external plugin cannot

send on the same connection, cannot intercept the middleware chain,
and cannot learn which OpenID a

message came from. Starting a second gateway with the same
AppID would race the first one for the ev

e from. Starting a second gateway with the same
AppID would race the first one for the event stream.
So the only clean option is a **minimal local fork**, and patch 0001 adds exactly two things:
| File | Change |
| `dist/gateway/middleware-setup.js` | one optional `preHandlers` argument, inserted at the **front*

* of the middleware chain |
| `dist/gateway/bootstrap.js` | `ctx.provide('qqbot', { setMessagePreHan
dler, sender, replyTargetFor, manager })` |

No existing statement is modified, and a host that never calls the extension point behaves
exactly a

s before. Rollback is one dependency range in the profile manifest.
Full evidence in `patches/0001-q
qbot-extension-point.md`.
## Quick start

Prerequisites: DSH with the Web profile, the stock QQ plugin installed and already bound to
your App
ID, and DS Bot with your team created.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Then allowlist yourself:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Editing `cordis.patch.yml` is picked up by DSH's config hot reload — **no restart needed**.
## Using it from QQ
| Command | Effect |

| `/管家` `/设计师` `/程序员` `/聊天` | switch which Bot you are talking to (persisted per OpenID) |
| `/团队` |

list the team |
| `/当前` | show who you are talking to |
| anything else | delivered to the current
Bot; its answer comes back to QQ |
## Configuration
All of it lives in **your** profile patch, never in this repository:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

`appId` / `appSecret` stay in the **official plugin's** config block, untouched. This project
never
reads, stores or logs them.
## Three Cordis/DSH surprises worth reading about
Both of these cost real debugging time, and both are now pinned by tests.

**1. `ctx.set` is not registration.** In Cordis 4, `ctx.provide(name, value)` registers a new
servic

e and returns a disposer; `ctx.set(name, value)` may only *overwrite* a service someone
already prov

ided, and otherwise throws `cannot set property "<name>" without provide`. Both
[该节后续省略]
## Security model

* **Fail closed.** An empty `allowOpenIds` refuses every peer.
* **No automatic grants.** A refused

OpenID is *written down* (so you can copy it into your
own config yourself) and nothing else. The br

idge never adds itself to the allowlist.
* **No credential handling.** `appSecret` stays in the offi

cial plugin's config; the bridge
owns no socket and opens no connection of its own.
* **Read-only on

DS Bot.** `state.json` is read, never written; its lock and atomicity are
respected.
* **No browser

shortcuts.** No `/api/bot`, no forged cookies, no bypassing the Web UI's auth.
* **Credentials are

scrubbed from every log line** (`lib/log.js`), and OpenIDs are shortened
unless `debug` is on.
* `sc
ripts/audit-constraints.mjs` checks all of the above mechanically.
